claim: Active zones consist of protein scaffolds that are tightly attached to the presynaptic plasma membrane.
source: Active zones consist of protein scaffolds that are tightly attached to the presynaptic plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about active zone structure.

claim: Active zones dock and prime synaptic vesicles.
source: They dock and prime synaptic vesicles, couple them to voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, and direct neurotransmitter release toward postsynaptic receptor domains.
evidence: This is established knowledge about active zone function.

claim: Active zones couple synaptic vesicles to voltage-gated Ca2+ channels.
source: They dock and prime synaptic vesicles, couple them to voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, and direct neurotransmitter release toward postsynaptic receptor domains.
evidence: This is established knowledge about active zone function.

claim: Active zones direct neurotransmitter release toward postsynaptic receptor domains.
source: They dock and prime synaptic vesicles, couple them to voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, and direct neurotransmitter release toward postsynaptic receptor domains.
evidence: This is established knowledge about active zone function.

claim: Simultaneous RIM + ELKS ablation disrupts active zone scaffolds.
source: Simultaneous RIM + ELKS ablation disrupts these scaffolds, abolishes vesicle docking, and removes active zone-targeted Munc13, but some vesicles remain releasable.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study and previous work by the authors.

claim: Simultaneous RIM + ELKS ablation abolishes vesicle docking.
source: Simultaneous RIM + ELKS ablation disrupts these scaffolds, abolishes vesicle docking, and removes active zone-targeted Munc13, but some vesicles remain releasable.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study and previous work by the authors.

claim: Simultaneous RIM + ELKS ablation removes active zone-targeted Munc13.
source: Simultaneous RIM + ELKS ablation disrupts these scaffolds, abolishes vesicle docking, and removes active zone-targeted Munc13, but some vesicles remain releasable.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study and previous work by the authors.

claim: Some vesicles remain releasable after simultaneous RIM + ELKS ablation.
source: Simultaneous RIM + ELKS ablation disrupts these scaffolds, abolishes vesicle docking, and removes active zone-targeted Munc13, but some vesicles remain releasable.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study and previous work by the authors.

claim: Hextuple knockout synapses (RIM1, RIM2, ELKS1, ELKS2, Munc13-1, Munc13-2) lacked docked vesicles.
source: The hextuple knockout synapses lacked docked vesicles, but other ultrastructural features were near-normal despite the strong genetic manipulation.
evidence: This is a finding from electron microscopy data in the current study.

claim: Hextuple knockout synapses had near-normal ultrastructural features apart from the lack of docked vesicles.
source: The hextuple knockout synapses lacked docked vesicles, but other ultrastructural features were near-normal despite the strong genetic manipulation.
evidence: This is a finding from electron microscopy data in the current study.

claim: Removing Munc13 in addition to RIM + ELKS impaired action potential-evoked vesicle fusion more strongly than RIM + ELKS knockout alone.
source: Removing Munc13 in addition to RIM + ELKS impaired action potential-evoked vesicle fusion more strongly than RIM + ELKS knockout by further decreasing the releasable vesicle pool.
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiology data in the current study.

claim: Removing Munc13 in addition to RIM + ELKS further decreased the releasable vesicle pool compared to RIM + ELKS knockout alone.
source: Removing Munc13 in addition to RIM + ELKS impaired action potential-evoked vesicle fusion more strongly than RIM + ELKS knockout by further decreasing the releasable vesicle pool.
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiology data in the current study.

claim: Munc13 can support some fusogenicity without RIM and ELKS.
source: Hence, Munc13 can support some fusogenicity without RIM and ELKS, and presynaptic recruitment of Munc13, even without active zone anchoring, suffices to generate some fusion-competent vesicles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in the current study.

claim: Presynaptic recruitment of Munc13, even without active zone anchoring, suffices to generate some fusion-competent vesicles.
source: Hence, Munc13 can support some fusogenicity without RIM and ELKS, and presynaptic recruitment of Munc13, even without active zone anchoring, suffices to generate some fusion-competent vesicles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in the current study.

claim: Munc13 proteins have a central role in neurotransmitter release mediated by synaptic vesicle fusion at presynaptic active zones.
source: Neurotransmitter release is mediated by synaptic vesicle fusion at presynaptic active zones, and Munc13 proteins have a central role in this process (Brunger et al., 2018; Dittman, 2019; Wojcik and Brose, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Active zone scaffolds contain RIM, ELKS, RIM-BP, Bassoon/Piccolo, and Liprin-α in addition to Munc13.
source: In addition to Munc13, active zone scaffolds contain RIM, ELKS, RIM-BP, Bassoon/Piccolo, and Liprin-α.
evidence: This is established knowledge about active zone composition.

claim: Active zone scaffolds form a protein machine that controls the speed and precision of synaptic transmission.
source: Together, they form a protein machine that controls the speed and precision of synaptic transmission by docking and priming of synaptic vesicles, by organizing the coupling of these vesicles to sites of Ca2+ entry, and by targeting transmitter release toward postsynaptic receptor domains (Biederer et al., 2017; Südhof, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mouse knockout studies established major roles for Munc13 in vesicle priming at central nervous system synapses.
source: Mouse knockout studies established major roles for Munc13 in vesicle priming at central nervous system synapses (Augustin et al., 1999; Varoqueaux et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Vesicle priming renders vesicles fusion-competent and adds them to the pool of readily releasable vesicles (RRP).
source: This process renders vesicles fusion-competent and adds them to the pool of readily releasable vesicles (RRP) that can rapidly undergo exocytosis upon action potential arrival.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vesicle priming.

claim: The functional RRP can be probed experimentally by applying stimuli that deplete it, such as superfusion with hypertonic sucrose solution.
source: The functional RRP can be probed experimentally by applying stimuli that deplete it, for example, superfusion with hypertonic sucrose solution (Kaeser and Regehr, 2017; Rosenmund and Stevens, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature describing the experimental method.

claim: When Munc13 is deleted, release competence of vesicles is abolished or strongly decreased across all tested synapses in multiple model organisms, including mouse, Drosophila melanogaster, and Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: When Munc13 is deleted, release competence of vesicles is abolished or strongly decreased across all tested synapses in multiple model organisms, including mouse, Drosophila melanogaster, and Caenorhabditis elegans (Aravamudan et al., 1999; Augustin et al., 1999; Richmond et al., 1999; Varoqueaux et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Munc13 ablation results in an almost complete loss of docked vesicles, as defined by plasma membrane attachment in electron micrographs.
source: Munc13 ablation also results in an almost complete loss of docked vesicles, as defined by plasma membrane attachment in electron micrographs (Hammarlund et al., 2007; Imig et al., 2014; Siksou et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Vesicle docking and priming are morphological and functional states that correspond to release competence.
source: These findings led to the model that vesicle docking and priming are morphological and functional states that correspond to release competence, a notion that is supported by similar correlations upon ablation of SNARE proteins (Chen et al., 2021; Hammarlund et al., 2007; Imig et al., 2014; Kaeser and Regehr, 2017).
evidence: This is a model supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Munc13s mediate the resupply of fusion-competent vesicles as they are spent during synaptic activity and thereby control short-term plasticity and recovery from synaptic depression.
source: Due to their core function in vesicle priming, Munc13s mediate the resupply of fusion-competent vesicles as they are spent during synaptic activity and thereby control short-term plasticity and recovery from synaptic depression (Lipstein et al., 2013; Lipstein et al., 2021; Rosenmund et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Munc13 nano-assemblies may account for secretory hotspots and recruit the SNARE protein syntaxin-1.
source: Furthermore, Munc13 nano-assemblies may account for secretory hotspots and recruit the SNARE protein syntaxin-1 (Reddy-Alla et al., 2017; Sakamoto et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Simultaneous deletion of RIM and ELKS in hippocampal neurons strongly disrupts active zone protein assemblies with subsequent loss of Munc13, RIM-BP, Piccolo, and Bassoon.
source: We simultaneously deleted RIM1, RIM2, ELKS1 and ELKS2, which resulted in a loss of RIM, ELKS, and Munc13, and in strong decreases of Bassoon, Piccolo, and RIM-BP levels at active zones (Tan et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2016; Wong et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Disruption of active zone assembly by RIM + ELKS knockout led to a near-complete loss of synaptic vesicle docking as studied by electron microscopy.
source: This disruption of active zone assembly led to a near-complete loss of synaptic vesicle docking as studied by electron microscopy and to an ~85% decrease in single action potential-evoked exocytosis as assessed electrophysiologically.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: RIM + ELKS knockout led to an ~85% decrease in single action potential-evoked exocytosis.
source: This disruption of active zone assembly led to a near-complete loss of synaptic vesicle docking as studied by electron microscopy and to an ~85% decrease in single action potential-evoked exocytosis as assessed electrophysiologically.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: After RIM + ELKS deletion, up to ~35% of release evoked by hypertonic sucrose remained under the tested experimental conditions.
source: However, some transmitter release persisted: up to ~35% of release evoked by hypertonic sucrose and ~50% of spontaneous release events remained under the tested experimental conditions, increasing extracellular Ca2+ to increase vesicular release probability p strongly enhanced single action potential-evoked release, and stimulus trains released vesicles surprisingly efficiently (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: After RIM + ELKS deletion, ~50% of spontaneous release events remained.
source: However, some transmitter release persisted: up to ~35% of release evoked by hypertonic sucrose and ~50% of spontaneous release events remained under the tested experimental conditions, increasing extracellular Ca2+ to increase vesicular release probability p strongly enhanced single action potential-evoked release, and stimulus trains released vesicles surprisingly efficiently (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Some releasable vesicles persisted after RIM + ELKS knockout despite the loss of most docked vesicles.
source: Hence, some releasable vesicles persisted despite the loss of most docked vesicles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data cited from previous work.

claim: Docking and priming are independent processes mediated by distinct molecular functions of Munc13.
source: These findings supported alternative mechanistic models in which docking and priming are independent processes mediated by distinct molecular functions of Munc13 (Kaeser and Regehr, 2017).
evidence: This is a model supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Artificial retargeting of Munc13 to synaptic vesicles rather than to active zones increased vesicle fusogenicity but not docking in mutants that lack most RIM and ELKS sequences and docked vesicles.
source: Further support for this model came from experiments with artificial retargeting of Munc13 to synaptic vesicles rather than to active zones, which increased vesicle fusogenicity but not docking in mutants that lack most RIM and ELKS sequences and docked vesicles (Tan et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Non-docked vesicles can contribute to the functional RRP after removal of RIM and ELKS.
source: Together, these findings suggest that non-docked vesicles can contribute to the functional RRP after removal of RIM and ELKS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cited data.

claim: Action potential-evoked excitatory transmission was strongly impaired in cKOR+E neurons.
source: Action potential-evoked excitatory transmission was monitored via NMDA receptors (NMDARs) to prevent the strong reverberant activity that is induced by stimulation of these neuronal networks when AMPA receptors (AMPARs) are not blocked.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B-C with sample traces and quantification.

claim: Munc13-1 was largely lost from the active zone area of cKOR+E synapses.
source: Based on these analyses, Munc13-1 was largely lost from the active zone area of cKOR+E synapses.
evidence: This is based on STED microscopy data shown in Figure 1G-K.

claim: Munc13-1 was ablated efficiently in cKOM neurons.
source: Munc13-1 was ablated efficiently in cKOM neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–F), with the leftover signal not distinguishable from background levels that are typically observed in this approach (Held et al., 2020; Nyitrai et al., 2020; Wong et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on STED microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–F.

claim: The remaining Munc13-1 signal was somewhat higher in cKOR+E synapses compared to cKOM synapses.
source: When we compared Munc13-1 levels in cKOR+E and cKOM synapses, the remaining signal was somewhat higher in cKOR+E synapses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is based on STED microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The higher Munc13-1 levels in cKOR+E synapses did not arise from a peak at the position of the active zone area.
source: These higher levels did not arise from a peak at the position of the active zone area (around –70 to –20 nm) (Tan et al., 2022; Wong et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on STED microscopy data analysis with citations to previous work.

claim: Munc13-1 levels appeared higher more broadly throughout the presynaptic bouton in cKOR+E synapses compared to cKOM synapses.
source: Instead, Munc13-1 levels appeared higher more broadly, and the ratio of Munc13-1 at cKOR+E vs. cKOM synapses shifted upward throughout the presynaptic bouton (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is based on STED microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: There was some release left at Munc13 knockout synapses.
source: As observed before in autaptic cultures (Banerjee et al., 2022), there was some release left at these Munc13 knockout synapses (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and cited previous work.

claim: The remaining release at Munc13 knockout synapses is likely due to the very small amount of remaining Munc13-1 when using this conditional allele.
source: This is likely due to the very small amount of remaining Munc13-1 when using this conditional allele (Banerjee et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an inference based on a citation to previous work.

claim: Some Munc13-1 might remain in nerve terminals of cKOR+E synapses.
source: Altogether, our data indicate that some Munc13-1 might remain in nerve terminals of cKOR+E synapses, but the remaining Munc13 is not efficiently concentrated in the active zone area apposed to the PSD, supporting previous data on RIM-mediated recruitment of Munc13 to the active zone (Andrews-Zwilling et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data with a citation to previous work.

claim: The remaining Munc13 in cKOR+E synapses is not efficiently concentrated in the active zone area apposed to the PSD.
source: Altogether, our data indicate that some Munc13-1 might remain in nerve terminals of cKOR+E synapses, but the remaining Munc13 is not efficiently concentrated in the active zone area apposed to the PSD, supporting previous data on RIM-mediated recruitment of Munc13 to the active zone (Andrews-Zwilling et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data with a citation to previous work.

claim: RIM1 and Munc13-1 were effectively removed from active zones of cKOR+E+M neurons.
source: We first used STED microscopy to analyze the localization and levels of RIM1 and Munc13-1 . RIM1 and Munc13-1 were effectively removed from active zones of cKOR+E+M neurons (Figure 2B–K, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on STED microscopy data shown in Figure 2B–K and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Synapse formation is intact in the absence of RIM1, RIM2, ELKS1, ELKS2, Munc13-1, and Munc13-2.
source: This indicates that synapse formation is intact in the absence of the tested active zone proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Synaptophysin puncta analysis shown in Figure 2L–O.

claim: Simultaneous deletion of RIM, ELKS, and Munc13 abolished vesicle docking.
source: Simultaneous deletion of RIM, ELKS, and Munc13 abolished vesicle docking (Figure 3A and B) similar to RIM + ELKS ablation (Tan et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3A and B with citations to previous work.

claim: Bouton size was unchanged in cKOR+E+M neurons.
source: While bouton size was unchanged (Figure 3D), there was a small decrease in vesicle numbers and a mild increase in the length of the PSD in cKOR+E+M neurons (Figure 3C and E).
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There was a small decrease in vesicle numbers in cKOR+E+M neurons.
source: While bouton size was unchanged (Figure 3D), there was a small decrease in vesicle numbers and a mild increase in the length of the PSD in cKOR+E+M neurons (Figure 3C and E).
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There was a mild increase in the length of the PSD in cKOR+E+M neurons.
source: While bouton size was unchanged (Figure 3D), there was a small decrease in vesicle numbers and a mild increase in the length of the PSD in cKOR+E+M neurons (Figure 3C and E).
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Nerve terminals and synaptic appositions form and are overall ultrastructurally near-normal apart from a loss of docked vesicles despite the strong genetic manipulation with deletions of RIM1, RIM2, ELKS1, ELKS2, Munc13-1 and Munc13-2.
source: Altogether, however, the morphological analyses, including STED, confocal and electron microscopy, establish that nerve terminals and synaptic appositions form and are overall ultrastructurally near-normal apart from a loss of docked vesicles despite the strong genetic manipulation with deletions of RIM1, RIM2, ELKS1, ELKS2, Munc13-1 and Munc13-2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the morphological data.

claim: The frequencies of mEPSCs and mIPSCs were robustly decreased in cKOR+E+M neurons compared to controlR+E+M neurons.
source: The frequencies of mEPSCs and mIPSCs were robustly decreased in cKOR+E+M neurons compared to controlR+E+M neurons, while their amplitudes remained unchanged (Figure 4A–F).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4A–F.

claim: The amplitudes of mEPSCs and mIPSCs remained unchanged in cKOR+E+M neurons compared to controlR+E+M neurons.
source: The frequencies of mEPSCs and mIPSCs were robustly decreased in cKOR+E+M neurons compared to controlR+E+M neurons, while their amplitudes remained unchanged (Figure 4A–F).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4A–F.

claim: Vesicle release is impaired in cKOR+E+M neurons.
source: Hence, vesicle release is impaired, but postsynaptic neurotransmitter detection is in essence intact in cKOR+E+M neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mEPSC and mIPSC data.

claim: Postsynaptic neurotransmitter detection is in essence intact in cKOR+E+M neurons.
source: Hence, vesicle release is impaired, but postsynaptic neurotransmitter detection is in essence intact in cKOR+E+M neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mEPSC and mIPSC amplitude data.

claim: cKOR+E+M neurons had very strong reductions in evoked release at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses compared to controlR+E+M neurons.
source: The cKOR+E+M neurons had very strong reductions in evoked release, both at excitatory (Figure 4G and H) and inhibitory (Figure 4I–K) synapses compared to controlR+E+M neurons.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4G–K.

claim: For both excitatory and inhibitory synapses, Munc13 knockout in addition to RIM + ELKS knockout decreased the remaining PSCs by ~40–50% compared to RIM + ELKS knockout only.
source: These analyses revealed that for both excitatory and inhibitory synapses, Munc13 knockout in addition to RIM + ELKS knockout decreased the remaining PSCs by ~40–50% compared to RIM + ELKS knockout only (Figure 4L and M).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4L and M.

claim: The remaining neurotransmitter release after RIM and ELKS knockout depends at least partially on the presence of Munc13-1 and Munc13-2.
source: Altogether, however, the data establish that the remaining neurotransmitter release after RIM and ELKS knockout depends at least partially on the presence of Munc13-1 and Munc13-2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiology data.

claim: Deletion of Munc13 on top of RIM and ELKS revealed an additional decrease in the functional RRP, with an almost complete loss of releasable vesicles at excitatory cKOR+E+M synapses.
source: Deletion of Munc13 on top of RIM and ELKS revealed an additional decrease, with an almost complete loss of releasable vesicles at excitatory cKOR+E+M synapses and an >80% reduction at inhibitory cKOR+E+M synapses (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: This is based on hypertonic sucrose application data shown in Figure 5E–H.

claim: Deletion of Munc13 on top of RIM and ELKS revealed an >80% reduction in the functional RRP at inhibitory cKOR+E+M synapses.
source: Deletion of Munc13 on top of RIM and ELKS revealed an additional decrease, with an almost complete loss of releasable vesicles at excitatory cKOR+E+M synapses and an >80% reduction at inhibitory cKOR+E+M synapses (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: This is based on hypertonic sucrose application data shown in Figure 5E–H.

claim: cKOR+E+M neurons had a significantly smaller RRP size than cKOR+E neurons in both excitatory and inhibitory synapse types.
source: Comparison of these two genotypes by a standard statistical approach showed that cKOR+E+M neurons had a significantly smaller RRP size than cKOR+E neurons in both synapse types (Figure 5I and J).
evidence: This is based on hypertonic sucrose application data shown in Figure 5I and J.

claim: The fusion competence of vesicles that remains after active zone disruption by RIM + ELKS knockout is mediated at least in part by Munc13.
source: We conclude that the fusion competence of vesicles that remains after active zone disruption by RIM + ELKS knockout is mediated at least in part by Munc13.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RRP data.

claim: Vesicles that remain fusion-competent after RIM + ELKS knockout are undocked, but likely associated with Munc13 at some distance away from the active zone.
source: Because Munc13 is not active zone-anchored and docked vesicles are barely detectable in cKOR+E neurons, these vesicles are undocked, but likely associated with Munc13 at some distance away from the active zone.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data.

claim: Paired pulse ratios are inversely correlated with vesicular release probability p.
source: Paired pulse ratios are inversely correlated with p (Zucker and Regehr, 2002) and strongly increased at short interstimulus intervals after knockout of RIM and ELKS at excitatory and inhibitory synapses (Figure 6A–D; Tan et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Paired pulse ratios strongly increased at short interstimulus intervals after knockout of RIM and ELKS at excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
source: Paired pulse ratios are inversely correlated with p (Zucker and Regehr, 2002) and strongly increased at short interstimulus intervals after knockout of RIM and ELKS at excitatory and inhibitory synapses (Figure 6A–D; Tan et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6A–D with citations to previous work.

claim: In cKOR+E+M neurons, vesicular release probability p was strongly decreased, illustrated by robust increases in EPSC and IPSC paired pulse ratios.
source: In cKOR+E+M neurons, p was also strongly decreased, illustrated by robust increases in EPSC and IPSC paired pulse ratios (Figure 6E–H), to an extent that is overall very similar to cKOR+E neurons.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6E–H.

claim: Munc13 knockout in addition to RIM and ELKS did not further decrease vesicular release probability p.
source: Comparison of genotypes through standard statistical methods or hierarchical bootstrap supported the conclusion that Munc13 knockout in addition to RIM and ELKS did not further decrease p, as effects in cKOR+E synapses and in cKOR+E+M synapses were indistinguishable (Figure 6I–L).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6I–L.

claim: The remaining Munc13 at cKOR+E synapses is sufficient to maintain a small functional RRP.
source: Hence, while the remaining Munc13 at cKOR+E synapses is sufficient to maintain a small functional RRP, it does not enhance vesicular release probability of these vesicles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RRP and paired pulse ratio data.

claim: The remaining Munc13 at cKOR+E synapses does not enhance vesicular release probability of these vesicles.
source: Hence, while the remaining Munc13 at cKOR+E synapses is sufficient to maintain a small functional RRP, it does not enhance vesicular release probability of these vesicles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the paired pulse ratio data.

claim: The transmitter release that remains after active zone disruption upon RIM and ELKS deletion depends at least in part on Munc13.
source: Our data reveal that the transmitter release that remains after active zone disruption upon RIM and ELKS deletion depends at least in part on Munc13.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in the current study.

claim: Munc13 might render some vesicles fusion-competent in the absence of RIM and when Munc13 is not anchored at the active zone.
source: Thus, Munc13 might render some vesicles fusion-competent in the absence of RIM and when Munc13 is not anchored at the active zone.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in the current study.

claim: This mechanism of Munc13 rendering vesicles fusion-competent without RIM and active zone anchoring is inefficient as it only maintains a fraction of the functional RRP of a wildtype synapse.
source: This mechanism, however, is inefficient as it only maintains a fraction of the functional RRP of a wildtype synapse.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in the current study.

claim: The functional RRP after RIM + ELKS knockout can be further boosted by re-expressing RIM zinc finger domains without enhancing vesicle docking.
source: We recently established that the functional RRP after RIM + ELKS knockout can be further boosted by re-expressing RIM zinc finger domains without enhancing vesicle docking (Tan et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: When the RIM zinc finger domain was expressed in RIM + ELKS knockout neurons, it co-localized with the vesicle cluster and was not concentrated at the active zone.
source: When the RIM zinc finger domain was expressed in RIM + ELKS knockout neurons, it co-localized with the vesicle cluster, it was not concentrated at the active zone, and it recruited Munc13 to the vesicle cluster.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The RIM zinc finger domain recruited Munc13 to the vesicle cluster in RIM + ELKS knockout neurons.
source: When the RIM zinc finger domain was expressed in RIM + ELKS knockout neurons, it co-localized with the vesicle cluster, it was not concentrated at the active zone, and it recruited Munc13 to the vesicle cluster.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Munc13 can enhance vesicle fusogenicity through association with non-docked vesicles, at least when this association is generated artificially.
source: Hence, Munc13 can enhance vesicle fusogenicity through association with non-docked vesicles, at least when this association is generated artificially.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cited data.

claim: Munc13-1 is barely detectable at active zones after RIM + ELKS knockout, while some Munc13 is present at synapses.
source: Here, we show that the remaining fusion in RIM + ELKS knockouts depends at least in part on Munc13 (Figures 4 and 5), but that Munc13-1 is barely detectable at active zones, while some Munc13 is present at synapses.
evidence: This is based on data shown in Figures 4 and 5 and STED microscopy data.

claim: Endogenous Munc13 can be near vesicles and enhance their fusogenicity even if Munc13 is not active zone-anchored.
source: These data indicate that endogenous Munc13 can be near vesicles and enhance their fusogenicity even if Munc13 is not active zone-anchored.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in the current study.

claim: Munc13 on non-docked vesicles might mediate the remaining fusion through generation of a pool of vesicles that can be rapidly primed and released upon stimulation.
source: Hence, Munc13 on non-docked vesicles might mediate the remaining fusion through generation of a pool of vesicles that can be rapidly primed and released upon stimulation.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the data.

claim: The rate-limiting step for generation of a functional RRP is the presynaptic recruitment of Munc13, even if Munc13 is not fully anchored and activated at the active zone.
source: Altogether, a model arises that the rate-limiting step for generation of a functional RRP is the presynaptic recruitment of Munc13, even if Munc13 is not fully anchored and activated at the active zone.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the data in the current study.

claim: RIM recruits Munc13 to active zones and activates it through binding of the RIM zinc finger to Munc13 C2A domains.
source: Previous work established that RIM recruits Munc13 to active zones and activates it. This mechanism operates through binding of the RIM zinc finger to Munc13 C2A domains, which is necessary for rendering Munc13 monomeric and active in fusion (Andrews-Zwilling et al., 2006; Betz et al., 2001; Brockmann et al., 2020; Camacho et al., 2017; Deng et al., 2011; Dulubova et al., 2005; Lu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Binding of the RIM zinc finger to Munc13 C2A domains is necessary for rendering Munc13 monomeric and active in fusion.
source: Previous work established that RIM recruits Munc13 to active zones and activates it. This mechanism operates through binding of the RIM zinc finger to Munc13 C2A domains, which is necessary for rendering Munc13 monomeric and active in fusion (Andrews-Zwilling et al., 2006; Betz et al., 2001; Brockmann et al., 2020; Camacho et al., 2017; Deng et al., 2011; Dulubova et al., 2005; Lu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Not all priming requires the RIM-mediated activation mechanism of Munc13.
source: This indicates that not all priming requires the RIM-mediated activation mechanism of Munc13, consistent with previous observations that many but not all RRP vesicles are lost after RIM knockout (Han et al., 2011; Han et al., 2015; Kaeser et al., 2011; Kaeser et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data with citations to previous work.

claim: Many but not all RRP vesicles are lost after RIM knockout.
